challenges.heading: What makes healthcare UX design harder than other SaaS design?

plan.title: Three users read the same record
plan.bodyHint: Patients, caregivers and clinicians each need a different first view of one chart. Caregiver (proxy) access more than doubled between 2020 and 2024, from 24% to 51% (ASTP/ONC). The fact-checker must confirm the base of that 51% before it is used; otherwise drop the number and keep the point. Design answer: role-based views, consent-aware proxy flows.

plan.title: Clinicians have seconds, not minutes
plan.bodyHint: 870 US physicians rated EHR usability at 45.9/100, and each point gained went with about 3% lower odds of burnout (Melnick et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2019). Correlation, not cause: say 'was linked to'. A new tool that adds clicks to that workflow gets ignored.

plan.title: AI output has to be checkable
plan.bodyHint: In the AMA survey, the top conditions physicians set for adopting AI were a feedback channel (88%), data privacy assurances (87%) and EHR integration (84%). Each one is a screen: a flag-this-answer control, a privacy statement at the point of use, and an in-EHR launch.

plan.title: Regulation shows up as interface copy
plan.bodyHint: HIPAA's minimum necessary standard, consent screens and notification text all have legal weight. Wellness apps outside HIPAA still fall under the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (amended, effective July 29, 2024). Under FDA's January 2026 general wellness guidance, wellness outputs avoid disease names and 'abnormal' labels.

plan.title: Patients juggle portals and devices
plan.bodyHint: 59% of US individuals had more than one portal in 2024, and only 7% combined them in one app (ASTP/ONC). App-based access rose from 38% in 2020 to 57% in 2024. Sign-in, account linking and record import are where a new digital health SaaS loses users first.

solutions.heading: How does healthcare UX design handle AI, FDA and HIPAA on the screen?

plan.title: Recommendation panels clinicians can verify
plan.bodyHint: Under section 520(o)(1)(E) of the FD&C Act, as explained in FDA's CDS guidance (revised January 2026), non-device CDS for health care professionals must let the clinician independently review the basis for a recommendation. That basis is a UX decision: inputs used, source, logic summary and known limits, shown next to accept, edit and dismiss. Add 'Confirm with your regulatory counsel'. We design to it; we do not classify products.

plan.title: Patient-facing AI with clear limits
plan.bodyHint: The CDS exclusion applies only to software for health care professionals, so a patient-facing symptom or triage tool needs extra care. Patterns: scope statements before the first question, escalation to a human, no diagnosis wording, and a visible 'what this tool cannot do'. Link chatbot UI design for conversational intake.

plan.title: AI interfaces ready for model updates
plan.bodyHint: FDA's final guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) for AI-enabled device software functions lets cleared devices plan model changes ahead. The UI needs version labels, 'what changed' notes for clinicians and stable controls, so a model update does not retrain users. ONC's HTI-1 source-attribute (model card) display for predictive DSIs is proposed for removal in HTI-5 (comment period closed February 27, 2026, not final). Write 'proposed', never 'removed'.

plan.title: Privacy patterns for protected health information
plan.bodyHint: Lock-screen and push notifications without PHI ('You have a new message'), masked fields in shared or screen-shared views, session timeouts with a save state, and consent and data-sharing screens in plain language. Name HIPAA and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule. Do not say the design makes an app 'HIPAA compliant'.

plan.title: Telehealth visits that start on time
plan.bodyHint: Pre-visit camera and mic check, a waiting room that shows status, one-tap caregiver or interpreter join, and an audio-only fallback. HHS OCR has guidance on audio-only telehealth under HIPAA. End with a plain-language visit summary. No claims about Medicare telehealth payment rules (they keep changing).

plan.title: Accessible components to WCAG 2.2 AA
plan.bodyHint: One design system with WCAG 2.2 AA built in: Target Size (Minimum) 2.5.8 at 24×24 CSS px, Accessible Authentication (Minimum) 3.3.8 so patients can sign in without a memory puzzle, Focus Not Obscured 2.4.11, and Consistent Help 3.2.6 for a 'call the clinic' link in the same place on every screen. Content that conforms to WCAG 2.2 also conforms to 2.1 and 2.0.

process.heading: How does a healthcare UX design project run?

plan.title: Workflow and risk map (1–2 weeks)
plan.body: Map each user role, where PHI appears, where AI output enters a decision, and which regulations your counsel says apply.

plan.title: Flows and patterns (2–3 weeks)
plan.body: Design role-based flows, consent and notification copy, AI review states and accessible components.

plan.title: Prototype and test (1–3 weeks)
plan.body: Prototype with realistic, de-identified sample data and test with 5 to 8 target users on real tasks.

plan.title: Handoff (1 week)
plan.body: Specs, a WCAG 2.2 AA checklist per component, and a pattern guide your engineers and quality team can use.

process.note: Durations follow the ai-ux-design-agency process (4 steps, 4–10 weeks, 5–8 test users). Do not claim that we recruit clinicians or have tested with clinicians or patients before: no case study shows it (competitors.json note on Elia Wellness). Use 'target users'. faqs.heading: What do digital health founders ask about healthcare UX design?
faqs.answerWords: 40-80 each, first sentence is the direct answer

plan.q: Can UX design make a health app HIPAA compliant?
plan.answerHint: No. HIPAA compliance comes from administrative, physical and technical safeguards, risk analysis and business associate agreements (a cloud provider that stores ePHI is a business associate, per HHS OCR). Design supports it with minimum-necessary views, PHI-free notifications, timeouts and clear consent. Note the HIPAA Security Rule update proposed January 6, 2025 is not final; do not describe its requirements as law.

plan.q: When does an AI feature make health software an FDA medical device?
plan.answerHint: Direct answer: when its intended use meets the device definition and no exclusion applies. For clinician-facing CDS, the four criteria in section 520(o)(1)(E) decide, and one of them is a UX question: can the clinician independently review the basis? Patient-facing CDS does not get that exclusion. Wellness-only products may fall under FDA's general wellness policy. Your regulatory counsel makes the call, and we design to it.

plan.q: Which accessibility standard should a US digital health product meet?
plan.answerHint: Design to WCAG 2.2 AA. HHS's Section 504 rule requires WCAG 2.1 AA for web and mobile content of HHS-funded recipients. An interim final rule (May 7, 2026) moved the dates to May 11, 2027 (15+ employees) and May 10, 2028 (smaller recipients). Section 508 uses WCAG 2.0 AA for federal ICT. ADA Title II covers public health systems. WCAG 2.2 AA content conforms to all three.

plan.q: Do wellness apps outside HIPAA still have privacy rules?
plan.answerHint: Yes. The FTC Health Breach Notification Rule covers health apps and connected devices not covered by HIPAA: breach notice within 60 calendar days, and unauthorized disclosure counts as a breach (amendments effective July 29, 2024). The FTC Act and state laws such as CCPA/CPRA also apply. Mention GDPR only 'if you also sell in the EU'.

plan.q: How do 21st Century Cures Act rules change a patient app's UX?
plan.answerHint: Patients can direct their records to the apps they choose. Certified health IT must offer standardized APIs, and information blocking rules apply to providers, certified health IT developers and HINs/HIEs. HHS OCR says a provider may not deny access just because the app does not encrypt data at rest. Design the connect-your-records flow, the scopes screen and a plain warning that HIPAA may not protect data once the patient moves it into a third-party app.

plan.q: How much does healthcare UX design cost with your team?
plan.answerHint: We publish service prices, not a separate healthcare price: MVP design $15,000–$50,000 (4–8 weeks), AI UX design $25,000–$90,000 (4–10 weeks), SaaS design $40,000–$180,000. Compliance-heavy flows, more user roles and platforms push a project up the range. Link the UI UX design cost guide, factors section. Do not invent a 'healthcare premium' percentage.
